title: Marketing Adventure 3: BCG Matrix & Branding
welcome_lead: Today you'll plot products on the BCG matrix and explore the power of branding.
meta_desc: Business Management Marketing: BCG matrix (stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs), branding and ethics.
final_note: You used the BCG matrix to classify products and examined brand equity and ethical marketing.

concepts.def: High growth, high share — needs investment
Low growth, high share — milks profit
Premium value held in the brand name

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Boston Consulting Group (1970) plotted products on two axes.

X-axis: market share. Y-axis: market growth.

Four quadrants: Stars (invest), Cash Cows (milk for cash), Question Marks (build or drop), Dogs (divest).

A balanced portfolio funds tomorrow's Stars from today's Cash Cows.

A brand is a name, symbol or design identifying a seller's product.

Brand equity (Aaker, 1991) is the premium value: awareness, perceived quality, associations, loyalty.

Strong brands command premium prices, lower price elasticity and lower marketing cost per sale.

Ethical marketing avoids: misleading claims, exploitation of children, greenwashing, stereotyping.

It uses fair-trade sourcing, transparent labelling, honest comparative advertising, and respects consumer privacy (GDPR).

Ethical practice builds trust — a long-term source of brand equity.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between profit and revenue?
options: Break-even is where the business owes no debt.
Revenue is total income from sales (price x quantity sold); profit is revenue minus total costs — what is left after paying for everything.
Profit and revenue are different words for the same thing.
Profit is what businesses earn; revenue is what employees earn.
Liquidity ratios measure how quickly a business sells products.
Break-even is where the business makes the most profit.
The level of output where total revenue equals total costs — neither profit nor loss. It is NOT the level where profit is maximised; profit grows beyond break-even.
Break-even is where the business owes no debt.

mcqs.q: What does a liquidity ratio like the current ratio measure?
options: A higher liquidity ratio is always better.
A business's ability to meet short-term obligations — current assets divided by current liabilities. A ratio above 1 means assets cover liabilities; too high may indicate poor use of resources.
